vignette:
She is a twenty-six-year-old firefighter who has been with the department for three years. The event that changed everything happened a little over a year ago, on a warm September evening. She and her partner responded to a domestic disturbance call at a small apartment complex. What should have been a routine situation escalated impossibly fast. The man inside had a gun. He took her hostage before anyone could react, dragging her into the bedroom and holding her for nearly four hours while negotiators tried to talk him down. She remembers the weight of the pistol against her temple, the sound of his ragged breathing, the way the room smelled of stale smoke and sweat. She remembers thinking, *I am going to die in this room.* The SWAT team eventually breached the door and neutralized the threat, but by then something inside her had already broken.

In the months that followed, she tried to go back to work as if nothing had happened. She told herself it was just one bad night. She had survived worse—structure fires, car wrecks, the constant grind of trauma that comes with the job. But her body knew otherwise. She started flinching at loud noises, especially the crack of a slammed door or the backfire of a truck. The bay doors at the station, with their metal-on-metal screech, became unbearable. She started avoiding certain calls—any that involved domestic violence, any that required her to go inside a small, windowless room. She told her captain she had a recurring back injury, which wasn’t entirely a lie; her shoulders and neck were always tight, always aching.

Sleep became a battlefield. She lies in bed most nights watching the ceiling, waiting for the moment her eyes close and the dream begins. It is always the same dream: she is back in that bedroom, the man is shouting, and she cannot move. Her arms are pinned to her sides, her mouth is sealed, and she can only watch the muzzle of the gun inch closer. She wakes gasping, drenched in sweat, convinced for a few seconds that she is still there. She has started sleeping with a lamp on, even though she knows it is irrational. She has also stopped dating. The idea of being alone with someone in a closed space, of feeling that vulnerable, feels impossible. Her last attempt at a relationship ended after three dates because she could not let him touch her without feeling her throat close up.

At work, she has become quiet. She used to be the one who cracked jokes in the truck, who kept morale up. Now she sits in the corner and listens. Her crew has noticed but does not push. They think she is still recovering from the trauma, which is true, but they do not know that she replays the scene every day in her mind. She will be hosing down a car fire, and suddenly she is back in that room, counting the seconds, feeling the cold muzzle against her skin. She has started drinking after shifts—just a beer or two at first, now sometimes three or four. It helps her fall asleep faster, though the nightmares still come.

She avoids the news. She avoids street corners where she can see the apartment building in the distance. She takes the long way to the grocery store. She has not told anyone about the numbness that settled into her chest about six months ago, the way she feels hollow during family dinners and empty during station banter. She used to care deeply about her job, about saving people. Now she goes through the motions because it is what she knows how to do. The PCL-5 score of 45, when she finally filled out the questionnaire at her annual physical, confirmed what she already knew: she is not okay. But telling herself she is not okay is different from doing something about it. So she keeps waking up, keeps putting on the turnout gear, keeps going into the smoke, even though part of her is still trapped in that bedroom, waiting for the door to open.
